intro: Ondine (Lent) is the first of Ravel’s three poems for piano in Gaspard de la nuit, in which a water spirit’s song is set beneath a tremble of piano chords. The pianist is Andriy Makarevych.

sections.label: A · Left-hand song under repeated treble chords
sections.mNote: The left hand plays the song below repeated treble chords.

sections.label: B · Arpeggios across the keyboard
sections.mNote: The water figures span a wider range between bass and treble.

sections.label: Dev · Melody within large arpeggios
sections.mNote: Large arpeggios surround the melody, which is set in chords.

sections.label: C · song over quieter arpeggios
sections.mNote: Quieter arpeggios surround the song as it comes back.

sections.label: Link · A voice without accompaniment
sections.mNote: Très lent: the water figures stop

sections.label: Coda · Rapid scales, C♯ major close
sections.mNote: Rapid scales give way to C♯-major arpeggios.

cues.title: Left-hand melody below chords
cues.text: The right hand plays closely packed chords, ppp. Below them the left hand has a slower melody, marked très doux et très expressif, several notes below the top of the piano texture.
cues.evidence: Durand score (1909), plate D. & F. 7207, p. 3: Lent, ppp right-hand chords and très doux et très expressif melody. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6a/IMSLP246875-PMLP02576-Ravel,_Maurice-Gaspard_de_la_nuit_Durand_7207_scan.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bertrand’s poem Ondine
cues.text: In Bertrand’s poem, Ondine touches a moonlit window and offers the man inside her ring. “Mon palais est bâti fluide, au fond du lac” — “My palace is built of water, at the bottom of the lake.” She asks him to marry her and become king of the lakes.
cues.evidence: Aloysius Bertrand, Ondine, reproduced before the movement in Durand’s Gaspard de la nuit (1909), from the Mercure de France edition of 1908. Second and fourth paragraphs; our translation.

cues.title: Wide arpeggios, chordal melody
cues.text: The arpeggios run from the low bass to the high treble. Ravel sets the melody in chords among them, with hairpins from pp to forte within a single arpeggio. The pianist must sustain the longer melody notes through the figuration.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 9–11: wide arpeggios, chordal melody and repeated crescendo hairpins.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ending of Bertrand’s poem
cues.text: In the final paragraph of Bertrand’s poem, printed before the movement in the Durand score (1909), the man tells Ondine that he loves a mortal woman. The water spirit sheds a few tears, bursts out laughing and vanishes in a shower down the blue windowpanes.
cues.evidence: Bertrand, Ondine, final paragraph, printed before the movement in the Durand score (1909).

cues.title: Unaccompanied phrase, Très lent
cues.text: Near the end the accompaniment stops. A single line is played in the middle of the keyboard, Très lent, with rests below it.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 13, final system: unaccompanied Très lent phrase.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing passage in C♯ major
cues.text: Both hands play a rapid passage, Rapide et brillant, which slows and gives way to ppp arpeggios in C♯ major. Bertrand’s last image is “mes vitraux bleus” — “my blue stained-glass windows” — with water streaming down them.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 14: Rapide et brillant, retenez peu à peu, ppp and return to C♯ major. Quotation from Bertrand’s Ondine, final paragraph, printed before the music in the 1909 edition; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Fermata, then unaccompanied Très lent line
transitions.how: The piano’s running figures climb to a held high note and stop under a fermata. The marking then changes to Très lent, and an unaccompanied phrase follows in the middle of the keyboard. The bass staff is empty.
transitions.evidence: Durand score (1909), p. 13, final system: fermata, followed by the unaccompanied Très lent line.

transitions.title: Rapid passage to the closing arpeggios
transitions.to: Coda · Rapid scales, C♯ major close
transitions.how: The bare phrase leads into a rush of notes in both hands, marked Rapide et brillant. Ravel then marks retenez peu à peu, and the pianist holds back gradually. C♯-major arpeggios return at ppp, au mouvement du début, and continue to the final chord.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 14: Rapide et brillant, retenez peu à peu, au mouvement du début and final C♯-major arpeggios.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
